sections.h2: Which offices handle Louisville property tax?
sections.html:
Louisville property tax is billed by the Jefferson County Sheriff. Since 2003 the city and Jefferson County have shared the same borders under the Louisville/Jefferson County Metro Government, so one set of county offices serves the whole merged area. Four offices touch a typical Louisville bill.

Offices that value, bill and collect property tax for Louisville addresses
OfficeJobLocation and phone
Jefferson County PVAValues property and takes exemptions and conferencesGlassworks Building, 815 W. Market St., Suite 400; 502-574-6380
Jefferson County Sheriff, Property Tax DepartmentCollects current-year billsFiscal Court Building, 700 W. Liberty St.; 502-574-5479
Jefferson County ClerkHolds delinquent bills after April 15527 W. Jefferson St., Suite 100a; 502-574-5884
Jefferson County Attorney, Tax DivisionRuns payment plans for delinquent taxFirst Trust Centre, 200 S. Fifth St., Suite 200N; 502-574-6331

The Sheriff's counter takes payments Monday through Friday from 8 AM to 4 PM. Mail goes to PO Box 34570, Louisville, KY 40232-4570.

sections.h2: What does the Louisville tax bill pay for?
sections.html:
One Sheriff's bill funds up to 13 taxing jurisdictions, and the office reports about $1 billion collected a year from more than 300,000 taxpayers. The list the Sheriff publishes shows how many layers sit on a Louisville house.

  • The Commonwealth of Kentucky and the Jefferson County Board of Education.
  • Louisville/Jefferson County Metro Government and the Urban-Service District.
  • The Louisville Downtown Management District, for parcels inside it.
  • A fire protection district, such as Okolona, Fern Creek, Fairdale, Pleasure Ridge Park, Jeffersontown/McMahan, St. Matthews/Lyndon, or Anchorage/Middletown.

The Jefferson County PVA counts 83 incorporated taxing jurisdictions, covering about 60,000 properties, and many of these smaller home rule cities send a separate bill. If your address lies in a suburban city, call that city's clerk about rates and amounts, because that bill is in addition to the Sheriff's. The PVA website has a contact list for each city.

sections.h2: What is Louisville like for someone selling a house?
sections.html:
Louisville is a river city that grew around a portage, and its housing stock reflects 250 years of growth. The settlement was founded in 1778 beside the Falls of the Ohio, and the city is now the most populous in Kentucky, with a Census Bureau 2025 estimate of 641,962 residents for the metro government's balance area.

The Ohio River shaped both the map and the market. In January 1937 the river crested at 57.15 feet, almost 30 feet above flood stage, and the flood covered 60 to 70 percent of the city. Afterward, residential growth shifted to higher ground in the east, and floodwalls now protect the low areas. Downtown sits south of the river, the airport is about 6.75 miles south of downtown, and industry clusters to the south and west of the airport.

Greater Louisville Association of Realtors data, as summarized on Wikipedia, shows the lowest median sale prices west of Interstate 65 in the West and South Ends and the highest north of Interstate 64 in the East End. Older neighborhoods around Old Louisville, Bardstown Road, Frankfort Avenue and NuLu were revived beginning in the 1980s. Weather matters too: Louisville has a humid subtropical climate, severe storms and occasional tornado outbreaks, and winter can bring ice that damages roofs and trees.

sections.h2: What do Census figures say about Louisville homes?
sections.html:
The Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 figures for Louisville/Jefferson County metro government (balance) put the median owner-occupied home at $233,900 and the owner-occupied rate at 60.7 percent, so about two in five households rent. Median gross rent is $1,120 a month, median household income is $66,849, and the typical commute is 22.5 minutes. The county counts 264,505 households, and 33.8 percent of adults age 25 and over hold a bachelor's degree or higher.

Averages hide the district differences. The same assessed value can carry a different bill in a fire district or a home rule city than in the Urban-Service District, so read the district lines on your own bill.

sections.h2: When are Louisville property tax bills due?
sections.html:
Jefferson County bills are mailed by November 1, based on the assessed value as of January 1. The 2026 bills are payable to the Sheriff from November 1, 2026 through April 15, 2027, according to the County Attorney's page.

  • November 1 to December 1: pay with a 2 percent discount.
  • December 2 to January 4: pay the face amount.
  • January 5 to February 5: a 5 percent penalty applies.
  • February 6 to April 15: a 10 percent penalty plus a 10 percent Sheriff's add-on applies.

If a due date lands on a weekend or a Sheriff's Office holiday, it moves to the next business day. No bill by the second week of November? Call 502-574-5479 for a duplicate, because a missing bill does not waive the penalties.

Payment options include cash, check or money order at the counter, mail, drop boxes at several County Clerk branches (Dixie, Fairdale, Highview, East and Westport) and an online portal. Online fees are $2.00 for an eCheck and 2.25 percent for cards, and the Sheriff's Office keeps none of that. The Sheriff accepts partial payments on the current year's bill while it is collecting.

sections.h2: How do I appeal a Louisville property assessment?
sections.html:
Use the PVA Online Conference during the annual inspection period, then appeal to the Local Board of Assessment Appeals at the County Clerk's office. For 2026, the online conference opened April 24 at noon and closed May 18 at 4 pm, a longer window than the 13-day minimum Kentucky law sets, which begins the first Monday in May.

  • Evidence helps: photographs, an appraisal, an insurance policy, repair estimates, construction costs, or a listing contract.
  • Comparable sales should be arm's-length and, for homes, within two years of the assessment date. The PVA does not count foreclosures, short sales or family sales.
  • A phone conference is available at 502-574-6224, with supporting papers due at least 3 days before.

The appeal to the board is filed at the County Clerk by one workday after the inspection period ends, or by the deadline on your online conference result. The board has three members, two appointed by the Mayor of Louisville Metro and one by Metro Council. The clerk's appeals line is 502-574-6915. A still-disputed result can go to the Kentucky Board of Tax Appeals.

sections.h2: What help exists if a Louisville owner cannot pay the tax?
sections.html:
Several options exist, and the best one depends on when the bill is late. Homeowners who are 65 or older or totally disabled get the $49,100 homestead exemption for the 2025 and 2026 assessment years by applying at the PVA.

The Jefferson County Attorney's Tax Division offers payment plans for delinquent bills. Plans for 2025 taxes opened on April 16, 2026, and the 2026 bills are not eligible for plans until April 26, 2027. An owner behind on an earlier plan must bring it current before 2025 can be added, and a written request may win a waiver of certain penalties and fees under 103 KAR 1:040. A bill on a payment plan cannot be sold at the tax sale.

In nine West End neighborhoods (Algonquin, California, Chickasaw, Park DuValle, Parkhill, Parkland, Portland, Russell and Shawnee), LHOME and the West End Opportunity Partnership offer a grant or 0 percent loan to qualifying residents who need to keep a residential bill current. The number is 502-882-8091.

sections.h2: What happens to unpaid Louisville property tax when I sell?
sections.html:
A bill unpaid after April 15 becomes a certificate of delinquency, a lien of record on the house. The County Attorney says approximately 40 percent in fees, interest and penalties is added at that point, and the certificate then bears interest at 12 percent a year. Unpaid certificates can be sold to a third party, and collection can include foreclosure.

At a sale, the seller usually pays the prorated tax for the months owned, and the buyer pays the whole bill. The name on the official roll cannot be changed mid-year, so a new owner pays a bill printed in the prior owner's name. Send a change-of-address form to the PVA for future bills. Check whether a certificate was bought by an outside investor on the clerk's online records, because then payment goes to the investor.

faqs.q: Who do I pay Louisville property tax to?
faqs.a: Pay the Jefferson County Sheriff's Office at 700 W. Liberty St., by mail at PO Box 34570, Louisville, KY 40232-4570, or online. After April 15 the bill goes to the Jefferson County Clerk. Smaller home rule cities send their own separate bill.

faqs.q: Is there a discount for paying Louisville property tax early?
faqs.a: Yes, 2 percent off when you pay between November 1 and December 1. The face amount is due from December 2 through January 4, then penalties begin.

faqs.q: Does Louisville have a separate city property tax bill?
faqs.a: No for most addresses, because the Sheriff's bill covers the Louisville Metro government and the Urban-Service District. Addresses inside one of the 83 smaller incorporated cities in the county receive an additional bill from that city.

faqs.q: How do I contest my Louisville assessment?
faqs.a: Complete the PVA Online Conference during the inspection period that begins the first Monday in May. If you disagree with the result, file with the Jefferson County Clerk for a Local Board of Assessment Appeals hearing by one workday after the period ends.

faqs.q: Can I set up a payment plan for delinquent Louisville property tax?
faqs.a: Yes. The Jefferson County Attorney's Tax Division sets up plans for delinquent bills at 502-574-6331. Current-year bills qualify only after they become delinquent, and a bill on a plan cannot be sold at the tax sale.
